Q: Semantic HTML, responsive layout and accessible interaction
explain:
A web interface starts with a document: headings establish topic hierarchy, landmarks identify navigation and main content, and form labels connect a question to its control. A button receives keyboard activation and a disabled state from the platform. Replacing it with a clickable div creates extra work for focus, keyboard events and semantics. Use a link to navigate to a resource and a button to change state. Explain validation errors next to their fields and keep user input after a failed request.

Layout needs to tolerate content rather than a particular screenshot. Start with one readable column, a bounded paragraph measure and flexible spacing. A grid can add a second pane when space permits; a preformatted code block may scroll inside its container while ordinary prose wraps. Test long identifiers, translated labels and text enlarged to 200%. A narrow screen should not require horizontal scrolling just to read an explanation. A fixed toolbar must not hide focused controls.

Accessibility is part of the interaction contract. A search dialog must have a name, move focus inside on opening, contain keyboard navigation while active and return focus to the opener. Do not move focus after each generated token. A polite status region can announce transitions such as streaming, failed and complete, while text accumulates in a separate region. Announcing every token overwhelms users. Icons and color can reinforce a status but must not be its only expression.

The local fixture uses a labeled form, scenario selector, actual buttons and a status region. It displays generated-looking text through textContent, preserving literal markup as text. A complete visual answer is intentionally different from the streaming state. Core documentation can remain readable without JavaScript even though the live exercise requires scripting. These guarantees should appear in the acceptance criteria before styling begins, so a later framework migration preserves the same user behavior.
example: A citation inspector opens over an AI response while the user navigates by keyboard. Record which button opened the inspector. Give the dialog a name and move focus to its first useful control. Make background controls inert and close on an explicit button or Escape. Return focus to the opener; preserve the response and scroll position. Result: The user can inspect evidence and resume the original task without losing context.
takeaway: If keyboard activation fails, inspect the element and event path before adding more key handlers. Check the accessible name and focused element; a visible label near a control is not necessarily programmatically associated with it.

Q: JavaScript promises, TypeScript boundaries and React snapshots
explain:
JavaScript executes a synchronous stack of work and resumes asynchronous callbacks through its event loop. Await does not turn a CPU-heavy loop into background work: the loop still blocks the page while it runs. A promise resolving to an HTTP response also does not imply a successful status. Check response.ok, validate the content type and parse the body according to a declared contract. Network failure, an HTTP error, invalid JSON and a valid business rejection need different user-facing recovery paths.

TypeScript describes the values your code expects; it cannot force an external service to obey. Treat received JSON as unknown until a validator has checked required fields, types, bounds and allowed states. A cast such as payload as Result changes the compiler's view, not the payload. Prefer a discriminated union for idle, loading, streaming, complete, failed and cancelled states. It rules out contradictory combinations such as loading=false with a hidden pending approval, but the network decoder still needs real checks.

React rendering is a snapshot of state. An event handler closes over the values from its render; calling a setter schedules another render rather than rewriting that closure. When the next value depends on the previous value, a functional update or reducer avoids losing concurrent updates. Store the minimal authoritative state and derive values such as canSubmit. Avoid separately storing the same response in component state, a cache and a mutable module global with unclear ownership.

Effects synchronize with systems outside rendering, such as a subscription or connection. Return cleanup that unsubscribes or aborts the old operation. Also guard which request owns a response: cancellation can race with an already delivered callback. The fixture's generation counter rejects stale events even after a new request begins. In a React port, keep that ownership token in a ref and drive visible state through a reducer. Keep rendering free of network side effects so repeated renders do not send duplicate work.
example: A user submits request A, quickly submits B, and A finishes last. Assign each submission an increasing generation number. Capture its generation before awaiting work. Accept a response only when its captured generation still matches the active one. Abort A to save work, but retain the generation check because completion may already be queued. Result: B remains visible even if A finishes after its cancellation request.
takeaway: Log a synthetic request ID, render generation and event sequence without recording the prompt. If an older answer overwrites a new one, compare ownership tokens; adding a loading boolean will not establish which request won.

Q: Browser trust boundaries, authentication UX and measured performance
explain:
Treat model text, retrieved passages and tool output as untrusted input. A model can repeat an HTML payload without understanding it. Render plain text by default; if Markdown is required, use an explicit parser and sanitizer configuration and restrict link protocols. Do not concatenate generated text into HTML, inline event handlers or script URLs. A claimed citation needs both a permitted source identity and server-side access control before a real document can be opened.

Authentication UX must explain session expiry and permission denial without exposing data. HttpOnly cookies reduce direct JavaScript access to a session token but require appropriate CSRF defenses and cookie settings. A bearer token held by JavaScript is exposed to successful script injection. Neither storage choice replaces object authorization on the server. After login identity changes, invalidate user-scoped caches and pending responses so one user does not see another user's retained state.

Performance work begins with a user-visible target and a measurement. A fast first token can coexist with a slow final answer, excessive rendering work or a broken cancellation path. Batch incoming updates to avoid rendering once per byte, and bound retained conversation/history. Lazy load large code examples and optional runtimes. A bigger bundle or unnecessary rerender is an engineering trade-off; optimize the measured bottleneck rather than adding memoization to every component.

Use a fixture to measure repeated starts, slow consumers, long text and malformed frames. Record the device/browser, input size, number of updates and timing window so a result can be reproduced. Keep a separate accessibility check because dropping announcements or focus indicators can make an interface seem faster while harming users. Production telemetry should record stage timings and aggregate outcomes without capturing complete prompts, document bodies or credentials by default.
example: A retrieved passage contains an image tag with an event handler. Render the passage as literal text in the fixture. If Markdown is enabled, verify sanitizer policy against the payload. Restrict outgoing citation URLs to supported protocols and permitted source routes. Test after a user switch to prove cached passages are scoped. Result: The passage cannot execute script or become an authorization bypass.
takeaway: If a user reports a previous account response appearing after sign-in, trace identity, cache key and pending request generation together. Purging visible text without invalidating a background request can allow the data to reappear.

Q: How do TypeScript types, generics, type narrowing and compiler algebra enforce sound contracts?
explain:
TypeScript layers a compile-time structural type system over JavaScript's dynamic runtime semantics. Unlike nominal type systems where types are differentiated by explicit declaration, TypeScript treats types as mathematical sets of assignable values. A union `A | B` represents the union of valid values, while an intersection `A & B` represents the subset of values possessing all properties from both types. Structural typing dictates that any object possessing the required shape satisfies the contract, regardless of its construction origin. To enforce nominal guarantees (such as differentiating a validated UserId from an arbitrary string), developers employ branded or tagged types using unique symbol tags.

Control flow analysis performs type narrowing across conditional branches. When a discriminator property, `typeof`, `instanceof`, or user-defined type predicate (`x is T`) is evaluated, the compiler shrinks the candidate type within that branch. Exhaustiveness checking leverages the bottom type `never`: by passing the unhandled remainder of a discriminated union to a function accepting only `never`, any unhandled union variant triggers a compile-time error when new variants are added.

Generics provide parametric polymorphism, allowing functions and data structures to operate over unknown types while preserving type relationships. Generic constraints (`T extends Base`) enforce minimal capabilities. Conditional types (`T extends U ? X : Y`) combined with the `infer` keyword enable type extraction and metaprogramming, such as unpacking promise resolutions or return types. Strict compiler flags—specifically `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`—close soundness gaps where undefined dictionary accesses or untyped variables would otherwise leak runtime runtime exceptions.
takeaway: Treat TypeScript types as compile-time set constraints. Use discriminated unions, type predicates and exhaustive never checks to ensure all runtime variations are handled at compile time.

Q: How do React Fiber reconciliation, concurrent rendering and hook state lifecycles coordinate UI updates?
explain:
React's runtime coordinates declarative UI state with browser DOM mutations through its Fiber architecture. A Fiber is an internal JavaScript object representing a unit of work and a virtual component instance. Fibers maintain linked relationships: `child` points to the first child, `sibling` to the next sibling, and `return` to the parent. This singly-linked tree structure allows React to traverse, pause, resume, and abort rendering work in small time slices without blocking the browser's main thread.

Rendering proceeds in two distinct phases: the Render Phase and the Commit Phase. During the Render Phase, React compares the current Fiber tree (`current`) against newly generated JSX elements to construct an alternative `workInProgress` Fiber tree. This reconciliation diffing algorithm operates in O(n) time using heuristics: two elements of different types generate entirely different subtrees, and stable keys preserve component identity across array reorderings. The Render Phase is purely computational, asynchronous, and interruptible.

Once reconciliation completes, React executes the synchronous Commit Phase. The host DOM mutations are applied, the `workInProgress` tree is swapped to become `current` (double buffering), synchronous layout effects (`useLayoutEffect`) fire to allow layout measurements before browser paint, and passive effects (`useEffect`) execute asynchronously after paint. Hooks are stored as a singly-linked list on the Fiber's `memoizedState` property; maintaining identical hook call order on every render is an immutable invariant that ensures state cells align correctly across renders.
takeaway: Distinguish between interruptible render computation and synchronous commit DOM mutations. Use transitions for deferred computations and respect the hook call-order invariant.

Q: How do resilient API integration, streaming fetch, abort controllers and cache synchronization operate?
explain:
Modern web frontends treat network I/O as a volatile asynchronous boundary. The native Fetch API departs from legacy mechanisms by resolving its promise on any valid HTTP response—including 4xx client errors and 5xx server failures; it only rejects upon catastrophic network failure or DNS resolution failure. Robust client wrappers must explicitly evaluate `response.ok`, parse typed JSON payloads safely, and translate non-2xx status codes into structured application errors with machine-readable codes.

To prevent memory leaks and wasted bandwidth, long-running or obsolete requests require deterministic cancellation. `AbortController` provides an `AbortSignal` that binds directly to `fetch`, `addEventListener`, or asynchronous promises. When component unmounting, tab switching, or rapid query typing supersedes an existing request, calling `abort()` terminates network transmission immediately. For temporary network partitions, exponential backoff with full randomized jitter prevents thundering herd congestion on backend services.

Consuming real-time streaming data—such as token-by-token generative AI responses—requires reading `response.body` as a `ReadableStream`. Coupling `ReadableStreamDefaultReader` with a `TextDecoderStream` processes chunked server responses progressively without buffering gigabytes into memory. Finally, caching layers (like TanStack Query or SWR) manage cache keys, optimistic mutations with rollback snapshots, background revalidation, and request deduplication to keep local UI state truthful against the remote authority.
takeaway: Check response.ok on all fetch calls, attach AbortSignal to every asynchronous request, and stream chunked responses progressively rather than waiting for complete payload termination.

Q: How do cross-window messaging, iframe sandboxing and multi-tab coordination maintain origin isolation?
explain:
The browser's Same-Origin Policy (SOP) prohibits scripts on one origin (protocol, host, port) from accessing DOM or JavaScript objects on a different origin. When legitimate communication across windows, tabs, or embedded iframes is required, `window.postMessage` serves as the controlled, auditable message-passing channel. Security hinges on two strict invariants: the sender must specify an explicit `targetOrigin` rather than `'*'`, and the receiver must verify `event.origin` against an authoritative whitelist before processing the message payload.

Embedding third-party content safely requires iframe sandboxing. The `sandbox` attribute restricts the embedded frame by default, removing script execution, form submission, popups, and same-origin privileges. While specific capabilities can be selectively re-enabled via flags like `allow-scripts` or `allow-forms`, combining `allow-scripts` with `allow-same-origin` on untrusted content completely destroys the sandbox boundary: an embedded script can programmatically remove its own sandbox attribute and take over the parent application.

For multi-tab communication within the same origin, the modern `BroadcastChannel` API provides a 1-to-many publish/subscribe channel with zero polling overhead. Alternatively, `SharedWorker` offers a shared background execution thread that can maintain a single persistent WebSocket connection across multiple open tabs. For cross-tab authentication synchronization, listening to `window.onstorage` events detects token invalidation and triggers immediate multi-tab logout.
takeaway: Never use '*' as postMessage targetOrigin. Always validate event.origin in message handlers and never combine allow-scripts with allow-same-origin on untrusted iframe embeds.

Q: How do frontend system design, state architecture and Core Web Vitals optimize applications at scale?
explain:
Enterprise frontend system design addresses the architectural challenges of scalability, performance, and organizational maintainability across large codebases. A robust frontend architecture separates concerns into clean vertical and horizontal boundaries: domain presentation components, application state management, data layer abstractions, and reusable design systems. Design tokens govern visual consistency across typography, spacing, and elevation, while headless UI primitives (such as Radix or React Aria) deliver accessible, keyboard-navigable behavior without styling constraints.

State architecture requires matching state to its proper scope. Local component state (`useState`) handles transient form inputs and toggles. Shared client state (`Zustand` or `Redux Toolkit`) manages cross-cutting UI state like sidebar toggles and modal managers. Server cache state (`TanStack Query`) governs remote entities, caching, and optimistic updates. Conflating server cache with local state causes data desynchronization and unnecessary global re-renders.

Performance optimization is guided by Google's Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP < 2.5s), Interaction to Next Paint (INP < 200ms), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS < 0.1). High-performance delivery relies on route-based code splitting via dynamic `import()`, tree shaking under ES modules with `sideEffects: false`, modern image formats (AVIF/WebP) with explicit aspect ratios, and DOM list virtualization (`react-window`) to render massive datasets at a steady 60fps.
takeaway: Architect applications with clear state boundaries: separate server cache from client UI state, split bundles at route boundaries, and actively monitor LCP, INP, and CLS metrics.

Q: How do frontend security defenses against XSS, CSP nonces and CSRF/CORS boundaries protect client applications?
explain:
Client-side security enforces defense-in-depth across the browser runtime. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) represents the preeminent threat, occurring whenever untrusted data is rendered into an active DOM execution sink (`innerHTML`, `eval`, `document.write`, or `href='javascript:'`). Modern frameworks mitigate reflected and stored XSS by escaping text nodes by default. However, when user-supplied HTML must be rendered (such as rich text or markdown), robust sanitization libraries like DOMPurify paired with the browser's Trusted Types API are mandatory to strip malicious payloads and event handlers before insertion.

A strict Content Security Policy (CSP) provides a cryptographic backstop against script injection. Rather than relying on vulnerable domain whitelists, modern CSP uses per-request cryptographic nonces (`script-src 'nonce-{RANDOM}' 'strict-dynamic'`) and disallows `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'`. Under this policy, injected script tags lack the required random server nonce and are terminated by the browser engine before execution.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is mitigated primarily by configuring the `SameSite` cookie attribute. Setting `SameSite=Lax` or `SameSite=Strict` alongside `Secure` and `HttpOnly` flags prevents the browser from attaching session cookies to cross-origin state-changing requests. Sensitive authentication tokens must never be stored in `localStorage` where any XSS vulnerability can extract them; storing tokens in `HttpOnly` cookies or memory-only scoped closures prevents script-based credential theft.
takeaway: Never trust client-rendered markup without DOMPurify and Trusted Types. Deploy strict nonce-based CSP, set SameSite=Lax on cookies, and avoid storing bearer tokens in localStorage.
